title: Limits of a Single Response
summary: Work through Limits of a Single Response.

blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Limits of a Single Response**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Test-Time Compute, § Limits of a Single Response
blocks.md: The repair agent (a later section) inspects the connection-pool implementation and receives a completed candidate patch. The invocation contract admits it as a candidate, yet the patch rests on an incomplete diagnosis. Client requests intermittently stall even after idle connections become available. Two distinct failure modes can produce this symptom: an aggressive timeout that aborts too early, or a lost notification when a worker thread returns a connection to the pool. When prompted, the language model proposes extending the timeout.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Allocation axes matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Depth, breadth, and feedback can spend the same output ceiling yet differ in critical path, retained KV state, and bill, and only feedback adds information the prompt and weights lack.

questions.q: The section **Limits of a Single Response** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A search tracks money, non-interchangeable work, wall time, and peak live state in separate accounts and reserves each request's maximum charge before dispatch, releasing it only on settlement.
A step check that rejects a fraction r of b children gives an effective branching factor b(1-r), so a tree stays finite on its own only when r > 1-1/b and otherwise needs hard caps.

Outcome checks execute a finished candidate while reward models only predict quality, and step checks prune failing branches early at the cost of false rejections and scorer input that grows quadratically without prefix reuse.
Depth, breadth, and feedback can spend the same output ceiling yet differ in critical path, retained KV state, and bill, and only feedback adds information the prompt and weights lack.
questions.hint: Re-read the excerpt and the section map: which idea is this section building toward?
questions.explanation: This section develops **Allocation axes**: Depth, breadth, and feedback can spend the same output ceiling yet differ in critical path, retained KV state, and bill, and only feedback adds information the prompt and weights lack.

questions.q: True or false: in the book's concept map, *Allocation axes* can increase candidate state controlled by *Copy-on-write block sharing*.
questions.hint: Think about which later idea this concept feeds.
questions.explanation: True. Allocation axes can increase candidate state controlled by Copy-on-write block sharing.
